It's sort of true though, racism is hard for a lot of people from historically dominant racial groups to discuss because their race has such a complicated history with other races. This means that many either try to show their "guilt" by acting overly friendly to marginalized groups and use specific compliments (which can be subtle racism) or be hateful and treat them as less than human because that's how history or family has influenced them to act. It can be a fine line at times. I'm of mixed heritage and look mostly like a member of the dominant group, so I've personally seen a lot of examples of both.

Even my parent, who is from the dominant group, sometimes exhibits subtle racism when not trying to sound that way. If I didn't witness firsthand the subtle things people say about marginalized groups so often, I probably wouldn't even notice.

True, but other races didn't colonize globally nearly as much as white populations and didn't have as widespread of a negative impact on so many different racial and ethnic groups. You would be hard pressed to find a racial or ethnic group that didn't have extremely severe issues with white populations historically.

In one country (can't really speak on another region right now), the majority of history is taught with a focus on white individuals, so the atrocities that occurred only between minority ethnic or racial groups are not covered nearly enough for a large number of other people here to know extensively about them. Therefore, many individuals (white and otherwise) who are born and raised here usually only see history through the lens of white individuals' past atrocities, which are what people tend to focus on. This means that white individuals here face significant pressure to avoid acting or being racist, given the well-known historical context of such behavior, fair or not.
